hints: Focus on what the 0.65 g really tells you, it is the mass of the gas inside the tube, so you need to link mass to moles.
Use $pV = nRT$ to find the moles first, remembering to convert $400 \text{ cm}^3$ to $4.0 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m}^3$ and $101 \text{ kPa}$ to $101000 \text{ Pa}$.
Divide the mass by your moles to get $M_r$ in $\text{g mol}^{-1}$, then match it to the familiar $M_r$ values of the noble gases.
walkthrough:
**Set up the ideal gas link**

Think of it like this, we know pressure, volume and temperature, so we can find how many moles are in the tube. The mass increase is just the mass of that gas.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$pV = nRT$$

**Convert units and find moles**

For this equation, pressure must be in Pa and volume in $\text{m}^3$. So $p = 101 \times 10^3 \text{ Pa}$ and $V = 400 \times 10^{-6} = 4.0 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m}^3$.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$n = \frac{pV}{RT} = \frac{(101000)(4.0 \times 10^{-4})}{(8.31)(300)} \approx 0.0162 \text{ mol}$$

**Calculate the molar mass**

Now use mass and moles to find $M_r$. This tells you how heavy one mole of the mystery gas is.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$M_r = \frac{m}{n} = \frac{0.65}{0.0162} \approx 40.1 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$$

**Match to the noble gas**

Argon has $A_r \approx 39.9$, which matches our result almost exactly. The others are far away, so the gas must be argon.

options.A: Argon is correct because $A_r$ of argon is 39.9, which agrees very well with the experimental $M_r$ of about 40 $\text{g mol}^{-1}$ calculated from $pV = nRT$.
options.B: Helium is false because $A_r = 4.0$. That would give a mass of only about $0.0162 \times 4.0 \approx 0.065 \text{ g}$, ten times too light. Students who pick this forget to check the size of $M_r$.
options.C: Krypton is false because $A_r = 83.8$. That would give a mass of about $0.0162 \times 83.8 \approx 1.36 \text{ g}$, roughly double the observed mass.
options.D: Neon is false because $A_r = 20.2$. That would give a mass of about $0.0162 \times 20.2 \approx 0.33 \text{ g}$, only about half the observed mass. It is a common trap if units for volume are not converted correctly.
